stories.headline: Iran offers seven-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
stories.dek: Tehran says it will reopen the waterway and admit U.N. inspectors if talks with Washington restart, but the White House has not accepted.
paragraphs: Iran has proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear talks with the United States. President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran would allow U.N. nuclear inspectors back in. The offer comes after months of war, sanctions and disruption to shipping and air travel.

The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow sea route used by a large share of the world's oil and gas shipments. Any closure raises energy prices and insurance costs far beyond the Gulf. At the same time, Iraq is asking Washington to exempt some airports from a U.S. ban on Iranian airlines for pilgrims, students and patients.

The main question is whether Washington will negotiate or resume military action. U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal that President Trump rejected the proposal and expects bombing to restart. Fighting tied to Iran's regional allies is also continuing, with Saudi Arabia reporting fresh Houthi drone and missile attacks.
stories.changes: If the strait reopens, oil shipments, freight insurance and some regional travel could stabilize quickly.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Iran and the United States are close to a full nuclear deal or that the wider regional conflict is ending.

cover.title: Iran offers to reopen Strait of Hormuz within seven days
cover.standfirst: Iran says it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz, accept U.N. nuclear inspections and restart talks with the United States under a seven-day plan. U.S. officials say President Trump has not accepted the offer, while attacks linked to Iran's allies continue across the region.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Make the cover almost entirely two blunt opposing coastlines of the Strait of Hormuz, rendered as heavy dark landmasses on off-white, with the water between them doing all the work: the channel must read first as the real strait and then, a beat later, as an opened zipper. Stage it mid-action so the gap subtly widens toward the top, with one coastline carrying a few simple zipper-tooth notches and the opposite side cleaner, enough to trigger the read without turning into a literal object; keep the lower third largely open water/off-white so type can sit cleanly across it.
art.note: Tense but not apocalyptic; limited inks in deep blue, rust red and sand.
art.second_beat: First it is the geography of Hormuz; then the same narrow passage snaps into an image of something being unzipped — the route reopening under tension, not just existing.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV begins first French state visit in 18 years
stories.dek: He is due to hold an open-air Mass in central Paris for about 600,000 people on Saturday.
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in France for a state visit, the first by a pope in 18 years. The trip brings the head of the Catholic Church to Paris for public events, including a large open-air Mass on Saturday. French authorities are preparing for very large crowds in the city center.

The main event is planned for Place de la Concorde and the nearby Champs-Elysees, where about 600,000 believers are expected. A papal visit to France is rare and carries both religious and diplomatic weight. For many Catholics, the Mass will be the clearest public moment of the trip.

Many details are still unclear from the early reports, including the full schedule, the length of the visit and any political meetings. It is also not yet clear what message Leo XIV will emphasize in France. Crowd management and security will be a major test as the weekend events begin.
stories.changes: If you are in Paris this weekend, expect major crowds, security controls and disruptions around the Concorde and Champs-Elysees.
stories.unchanged: This visit does not change French law or the pope's formal role in the French state.

cover.title: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Paris for first French state visit in 18 years
cover.standfirst: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in France for the first papal state visit there in 18 years. On Saturday he is due to celebrate an open-air Mass for about 600,000 believers at Place de la Concorde and along the Champs-Elysees, with heavy security and traffic disruption expected.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: A high, slightly distant gouache view over Place de la Concorde into the lower Champs-Elysees under a flat grey-blue Paris sky: the Luxor obelisk, the two great fountains, and the straight run of Haussmann facades make the location unmistakable. A tiny white popemobile has just entered the square, and from it the packed pale crowd spreads and streams up the avenue in one continuous shape that also reads, a beat later, as a white liturgical vestment or stole unfurling across the city; keep the lower third mostly quiet with wet open paving and soft reflections for type.
art.note: Calm civic scale, soft Paris light, pale stone and muted tricolor accents.
art.second_beat: First it reads as the scale of the Paris crowd; then the crowd resolves into the Church’s garment draped through Concorde and up the Champs-Elysees.

stories.headline: German investigators suspect GRU role in Munich arson attack
stories.dek: Two incendiary devices were thrown at a Munich construction site near defense firms Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing on Sept. 3.
paragraphs: German investigators believe Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, may have organized an arson attack in Munich this month, according to a new report in Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung. The case matters now because German officials are already tying another recent sabotage plot, at Leipzig/Halle Airport, to Russia.

On the night of Sept. 3, two incendiary devices were thrown from a moving car onto a construction site in Munich’s Berg am Laim district, near the headquarters of Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing. One device started a small fire and the other was defused. No one was hurt. Two Bulgarian citizens were later detained.

Prosecutors have not confirmed a Russian link and say the investigation is still open. It is also not clear who ordered the attack, whether the suspects knew who they were working for, or how it connects to a wider network. Germany has reported more than 165 suspected sabotage cases this year.
stories.changes: For readers in Germany and Europe, this adds to evidence that attacks linked to Russia may target transport, defense firms and nearby infrastructure, not only military sites.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Germany is under open attack or that every fire or drone sighting is part of a Russian operation.

cover.title: German investigators suspect Russian role in Munich arson attack
cover.standfirst: German investigators believe the GRU may have organized a Sept. 3 arson attack near the Munich headquarters of defense technology firms Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing. Two incendiary devices were thrown from a moving car, two Bulgarian suspects were detained, and prosecutors are still testing the Russian link.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Night at a Munich construction site in Berg am Laim, reduced to a flat plane of pale dirt, fencing, and a few unmistakable site elements, with the lower third left mostly empty for type. Across the ground falls one huge cold-blue shadow of an unseen figure mid-throw; from the shadow-hand alone, two fluorescent-pink burning bottles have just left the grip and arc into frame. Shape the head-and-shoulders of the shadow so it subtly echoes onion-dome architecture without turning into a flag, map, or caricature: the attack is visible, the attacker is only an implication.
art.note: Cold, tense, urban palette with sodium orange against deep blue-grey.
art.second_beat: First read: arson in action; second beat: only the shadow commits it, turning GRU suspicion into a literal covert presence on German soil.

stories.headline: Premier League clubs seek advice on possible Man City claims
stories.dek: Some clubs are asking lawyers if they could seek compensation if Manchester City are later found liable on the league's 115 charges.
paragraphs: Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice on whether they could claim compensation in the Manchester City charges case. The issue has surfaced because the long-running case could have financial consequences for rival clubs if City are eventually found to have broken league rules.

Manchester City face 115 Premier League charges, which the club deny. The case relates to alleged breaches of financial rules over a number of seasons. For other clubs, the basic question is whether any proven rule-breaking may have cost them prize money, places in competitions, or other income.

Nothing has been decided on compensation, and the charges case itself has not been resolved. It is not clear which clubs are taking advice, what legal route they might use, or whether any claim would succeed. Any action would depend on the outcome of the main case.
stories.changes: If you follow a Premier League club, this case could grow beyond points and titles into a separate fight over money.
stories.unchanged: Matches, league tables and past results do not change today, and no club has won compensation or proved a claim.

cover.title: Premier League clubs weigh claims over Manchester City charges case
cover.standfirst: Premier League clubs are asking lawyers whether they could seek compensation linked to Manchester City's 115 charges case. City deny the charges. No claim has been filed and the main case is still unresolved, but clubs may argue they lost money if breaches are eventually proven.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat hazard-orange ground, hang a single black-and-white medal ribbon dead centre, cropped high so it drops into the lower half of the frame. The ribbon has just been cut: the upper section remains taut from above, while the lower section is caught mid-fall, tipping away and dropping out of frame; at the severed point, add one crude hand-drawn black circle to force the eye to the cut. Keep the lower third mostly open except for the falling tail, so the action reads instantly and type can sit cleanly across it.
art.note: Sharp, skeptical mood; cool blues, off-white paper, and harsh black accents.
art.second_beat: First read: something valuable has been severed; second beat: a lost Champions League place is being pictured as a route materially cut away, which is exactly what clubs may claim compensation for.

stories.headline: Former City chairman calls for severe penalty if appeal fails
stories.dek: David Bernstein said a fine would not be enough if Manchester City lose an expected appeal over Premier League financial charges.
paragraphs: Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein said the club should face a severe punishment, not just a fine, if an expected appeal fails in its financial charges case. He spoke after reports said City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 Premier League charges, though the process is still ongoing.

The Premier League brought the charges in 2023, covering alleged rule breaches from 2009 onward. City have denied wrongdoing throughout. The case matters because the period under scrutiny overlaps with the club’s most successful era, when it won major domestic and European trophies and became the dominant team in English football.

No final punishment has been decided, and City say significant parts of the process remain incomplete and confidential. An appeal is expected if the club is formally found guilty. Ministers and politicians have called for the case to be resolved quickly, saying a long delay would damage trust in English football’s rules.
stories.changes: For football fans, the case is moving closer to a stage where points deductions, titles questions or other sporting penalties are being openly discussed.
stories.unchanged: Manchester City have not been finally punished, and the club is still contesting the charges through an unfinished legal process.

cover.title: Former Manchester City chairman urges harsh penalty if appeal fails
cover.standfirst: David Bernstein said money alone would not be enough if Manchester City lose an expected appeal over 115 Premier League financial charges. The club denies wrongdoing and says the process is still incomplete. Politicians and football officials now want a faster final decision.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat acid-green ground, place the Manchester City crest low and slightly right, large enough to read instantly by shape alone. From the top left, a thick, dark hardback rulebook hurtles diagonally down toward it, frozen a split second before impact; add one crude black marker X already slashed across part of the crest to suggest judgment is underway. Keep the lower third mostly empty apart from the crest so type can sit cleanly.
art.note: Sharp, uneasy, institutional mood; sky blue, black, off-white, and dull gold.
art.second_beat: First you see a book about to smash the City badge; a beat later you get that it is the rulebook itself — the charges becoming punishment.

stories.headline: Thousands remain missing a month after Nepal floods
stories.dek: One month after severe flooding in Nepal, many families still do not know who survived and face a long rebuild.
paragraphs: A month after major floods in Nepal, thousands of people are still missing and many families are living with deep uncertainty. The story matters now because the first month of search and emergency relief has passed, but the human toll is still not fully known.

Floods can sweep away homes, roads, bridges and whole settlements in a short time, especially in mountain valleys and river basins. In Nepal, that damage can leave communities cut off for days or weeks. Families often lose relatives, farmland, livestock, documents and the means to earn money.

It is still unclear how many missing people will be found, how quickly isolated areas can recover, and what support families will receive over time. Recovery will likely take months or longer. For many people, the hardest part now is waiting for news while trying to rebuild daily life.
stories.changes: For ordinary people, this means the disaster is not over when floodwaters fall, because loss, displacement and missing relatives can shape life for months.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all of Nepal is underwater or that every flood-hit family faces the same level of damage and delay.

cover.title: Thousands in Nepal are still missing after floods
cover.standfirst: A month after severe floods in Nepal, thousands of people are still missing and many families are waiting for news of relatives. Homes, land and local roads were damaged, leaving a long recovery ahead. Search efforts and basic support continue as communities try to rebuild.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Inside a temporary shelter in Nepal, show a sleeping area from slightly above: two rumpled blankets, a dented cooking pot, a tin plate, and a pair of sandals pushed near the bedding. In the middle, leave one clear human-shaped hollow in the blankets completely as untouched cream paper while everything else is cut in severe black hatching; a single hand at the edge of frame is lifting the blanket toward that hollow, still making space for someone who has not returned. Keep the lower third quiet with the bedding and floor plane simplified for cover lines.
art.note: Quiet, heavy mood; muted earth tones, slate grey, and river brown.
art.second_beat: First you read a family’s sparse shelter; a beat later the untouched body-shaped void and the hand adjusting the blanket turn the scene into the uncertainty of someone still missing.

stories.headline: China and US agree direct channel for AI incidents
stories.dek: After their summit in Washington, both governments said they will create a line to discuss AI risks and share views on stronger systems.
paragraphs: The United States and China said they will open a direct communication channel for artificial intelligence incidents after a summit between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping in Washington. The move comes as both countries say faster AI development could create new security and safety risks that need quick contact.

The White House said the two sides also set up a US-China dialogue on what it called super intelligence, or SI, to discuss AI's risks and benefits. Chinese state media later confirmed the hotline. Before the meeting, Trump said the topic would be discussed carefully. Xi said AI must remain under human control.

It is still unclear how the channel will work, who can use it, or what counts as an AI incident. The two governments did not say whether the talks will cover military systems, cyber attacks, or rules for advanced models. A hotline does not settle the wider US-China technology rivalry.
stories.changes: It raises the chance that Washington and Beijing can speak quickly if an AI system causes a serious cross-border problem.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the US and China now trust each other on technology or are easing their broader competition.

cover.title: China and the United States agree AI incident hotline
cover.standfirst: After a summit in Washington on Sept. 25, the United States and China said they will create a direct channel for AI incidents and start a separate dialogue on the risks and benefits of more powerful systems. Both sides have not yet explained who will use the line or what events will trigger it.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a pale blue seamless background, stage a single bright-red desk-phone handset at the far right edge with its coiled cord stretched hard across the frame to a matte-black AI server tower at the far left. The cord should plug directly into the server through a clearly improvised adapter point and snag into one loose knot at centre, so the line exists but looks newly rigged and not fully trustworthy; keep the lower third clean and empty for type.
art.note: Calm, official mood; limited red, blue, black and cream palette.
art.second_beat: First read: a US–China-style hotline; second beat: it is not phone-to-phone at all, but a crisis line hastily patched into a machine.

stories.headline: Police say Tasia Fortune was killed before staged hanging
stories.dek: A detective told a Jackson court that Fortune died in a drug dispute and her body was later hung in a tree.
paragraphs: Jackson police said in court Friday that Tasia Fortune was killed during a drug dispute and then hung in a tree to stage the scene. The testimony came at a hearing to decide whether one murder case should move toward a grand jury.

Fortune's body was found Aug. 3 behind an abandoned home in Jackson. She was Black, and the hanging drew wide attention because it resembled lynchings in a state with a long history of racist violence. Police have charged three Black men with murder.

Authorities still have not said exactly how Fortune died or why they believe her body was hung after death. One defendant has pleaded not guilty, another was arrested this week, and a third turned himself in Friday. The court hearing resumes Sept. 30.
stories.changes: Readers now know police believe the hanging scene was staged after Fortune was killed, not the cause of her death.
stories.unchanged: This does not answer every question in the case, and it does not by itself prove guilt against any defendant.

cover.title: Police say Tasia Fortune was killed before hanging in Jackson
cover.standfirst: A Jackson detective told a court Friday that Tasia Fortune was killed in a drug dispute and her body was later hung in a tree behind an abandoned home. Three men now face murder charges. The hearing on one case resumes on Sept. 30.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: A row of thin Mississippi trees stands in a weedy lot behind a shotgun house, all cut in strict vertical rhythm so the grove first reads as pattern. From a branch in one tree, a rope is being yanked sharply upward from off-frame by an unseen hand, the line still taut and the knot not yet settled, while nearby branches carry only harmless loops of kudzu and storm-torn debris; keep the lower third quiet with pale weeds and ground for type.
art.note: Quiet, severe, desaturated browns and grays.
art.second_beat: First you see a calm repeated grove; then one rope reveals a human act mid-staging, turning ordinary hanging debris into evidence of a manufactured scene.

stories.headline: US moves to secure last $93 million in Ukraine aid
stories.dek: The administration plans to obligate the final share of a $400 million military package before the Sept. 30 deadline.
paragraphs: The Trump administration plans to legally commit the last $93 million of a $400 million military aid package for Ukraine before Sept. 30. That matters because money not obligated by the end of the fiscal year can expire. Officials have already committed $307 million.

The money comes from the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, a Pentagon program that pays for weapons, equipment and support for Kyiv. Congress approved the package late last year. Once funds are obligated, they remain available to be spent later under the terms of the program.

It is still not clear exactly which equipment or services the final $93 million will cover, or how quickly contracts will turn into deliveries. This step protects the money from expiring. It does not settle wider questions about future US military support for Ukraine.
stories.changes: For readers, this means previously approved US aid for Ukraine is less likely to vanish because of a budget deadline.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean new aid was approved, or that weapons will arrive in Ukraine immediately.

cover.title: US secures final $93 million in military aid for Ukraine
cover.standfirst: The Trump administration plans to obligate the last part of a $400 million Ukraine military package before the Sept. 30 fiscal-year deadline. Washington has already committed $307 million. The move keeps nearly all of the congressionally approved money available for later contracts and deliveries.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a clean blue seamless, show a military cargo pallet wrapped in clear stretch film, viewed three-quarters from the front. The load is fully built except for one crisp rectangular missing block at the front corner; the clear film is already being pulled across that void, stretched taut over empty air, with one or two loosened packing straps curling outward so we catch the instant before the last gap is sealed. Keep the pallet large and slightly high in frame so the lower third stays mostly quiet blue for type, and strip away every extra prop.
art.note: Cool, procedural, restrained palette with navy, white, and muted yellow.
art.second_beat: First read: a military shipment being secured; second beat: the one missing compartment is the final uncommitted share, small against the whole but exactly what would otherwise be left behind.

stories.headline: Nor'easter strengthens as East Coast towns brace for flooding
stories.dek: States of emergency were declared in New York and New Jersey as coastal towns prepared for flooding, strong winds and power cuts.
paragraphs: A strong nor'easter moved toward New England on Friday, bringing storm-force winds, heavy rain and dangerous surf to the East Coast. Forecasters warned of coastal flooding from New Jersey to Massachusetts through Saturday. Officials canceled events, urged some residents to leave low areas, and prepared shelters.

A nor'easter is a coastal storm that often hits the Northeast in cooler months. This one was expected to hit hardest along the shore, with gusts near 60 to 65 mph on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket. Leaves still on trees could make wind damage and power outages more likely.

The biggest unknown is how high the water will get in exposed coastal towns and how long roads stay flooded. Local leaders warned some streets could see several feet of water. The storm was expected to weaken later Saturday, but damage, erosion and outages could last longer.
stories.changes: People along the Northeast coast may need to change travel plans, avoid flooded roads and prepare for power loss this weekend.
stories.unchanged: This is a serious coastal storm, but it is not hitting the whole Northeast with the same force and inland areas face less risk.

cover.title: A strong nor'easter threatens flooding across the East Coast
cover.standfirst: A strengthening coastal storm is bringing heavy rain, strong winds and high surf from New Jersey to Massachusetts. States of emergency were declared in New York and New Jersey, and some shore towns urged residents to leave low-lying areas before flooding peaks into Saturday.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint a coastal New Jersey kitchen at the exact moment the power has just failed: the refrigerator door hangs open but its interior light is dead, and a pair of unseen hands at the edge of frame is hurriedly transferring food into a blue cooler on the floor. A carton of milk is tipping out, freezer frost is already beginning to soften and drip, and beyond the sink window a flat sheet of gray floodwater has quietly replaced the street outside; keep the composition simple and the lower third mostly clear with the cooler, fallen items, and bare floor carrying the scene.
art.note: Cold, windy, steel-blue palette with a tense but ordinary mood.
art.second_beat: First you read an ordinary kitchen scramble, then you realize the real storm image is the dead fridge and the street outside already turned to water — the nor'easter arrives as consequence, not spectacle.
